# Why institutions — and why a firm should care {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Put it to the room

> Your firm bids to build a power plant in Kenya. **Name every international institution that could be involved** — as lender, insurer, co-investor, referee or competitor.

## Two answers

| | **Liberal institutionalism** | **Realism** |
|---|---|---|
| **Key text** | Keohane (1984), *After Hegemony* | Mearsheimer (1994/95), *The False Promise…* |
| **Why they exist** | Lower transaction costs; information; a longer shadow of the future | They reflect the distribution of power |
| **Do they constrain?** | At the margin — reneging becomes costly | Rarely — power wins when interests collide |
| **For the firm** | A loan, a policy, an award behave predictably | Read the shareholders, not the charter |

::: {.get}
The firm's question is not *which theory is true* but **which institution, on which issue, behaves like which.**
:::

### Regime shifting

Move the issue to **another existing** institution

Build a **new** one — the AIIB is the textbook case

# The Bretton Woods core {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## The IMF: who holds the votes {.scrollable}

| | |
|---|---|
| **Founded** | Articles adopted at Bretton Woods, 22 July 1944 · **191** members |
| **Lends to** | Governments — never to firms; its programmes set the firm's conditions |
| **Voting power** | **US 16.49%** · Japan 6.14% · **China 6.08%** · India ≈2.63% · Russia ≈2.59% · Brazil ≈2.22% · South Africa ≈0.63% |
| **The 85% rule** | Any quota change needs 85% of votes → **only the US can block alone** |
| **Reform** | 16th Review: +50%, **equiproportional** — no realignment; still not in force (deadline 15 Nov 2026) |

::: {.warn}
**Votes lag economic weight.** That gap is why the new institutions exist.
:::

::: {.muted}
IMF *Annual Report 2026*, App. IV (votes as of 30 April 2026); India–South Africa shares computed from vote counts. Accessed 16 Oct 2026.
:::

## WTO and OECD — the rules around the deal

| | What matters to the firm |
|---|---|
| **WTO** (1995 · 166 members) | Tariff bindings, non-discrimination. **No Appellate Body members since 30 Nov 2020**; 62 members appeal through the **MPIA** instead |
| **OECD** (38 members) | **Export-credit Arrangement** (1978): caps the terms ECAs may offer — China is not a participant |
| | **MNE Guidelines** (1976, updated 2023): complaints go to National Contact Points |
| | **Pillar Two**: 15% minimum tax on groups ≥ €750 m revenue |

# The World Bank Group as a business toolkit {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Five institutions, five things a firm can use {.scrollable}

| | Founded · members | For the firm |
|---|---|---|
| **IBRD / IDA** | 1944 / 1960 · 189 / 175 | **Contracts** — projects buy through international procurement |
| **IFC** | 1956 · 186 | **Co-investment**: loans in 88 local currencies, equity, guarantees; MCPP co-lending |
| **MIGA** | 1988 · 182 | **Political risk insurance**: transfer, expropriation, war, breach of contract, sovereign non-honouring |
| **ICSID** | 1966 · 159 states | **Investor–state arbitration** |

::: {.muted}
World Bank Group members page; ICSID/3 (16 Aug 2026). Accessed 16 Oct 2026.
:::

## The scale, FY2026

::::: columns

:::: {.column width="50%"}

### Finance and insurance

- **IFC**: US$32.0 bn own account; US$73.6 bn private capital mobilised
- **MIGA**: record US$10.6 bn issued, 60 projects; gross exposure US$41.4 bn
- **Guarantee Platform** at MIGA since 1 July 2024 — target US$20 bn a year by 2030

::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}

### Disputes

- **ICSID**: 1,118 cases registered; 363 administered in FY2026
- New cases: oil & gas 25%, mining 18%; 62% under BITs
- Denunciations: Bolivia 2007, Ecuador 2009 (back 2021), Venezuela 2012, Honduras 2024 (back 2026)

::::

:::::

## Procurement — and its other side

::: {.step}
**Procurement Framework** (1 July 2016): notices on UN Development Business and the World Bank site — the largest, least-noticed business channel.
:::

::: {.warn}
**Cross-debarment** (9 April 2010): a debarment over one year by the WBG, ADB, AfDB, EBRD or IDB is enforced by **all five**. More than 1,500 firms and individuals so far.
:::

**Who holds the votes?** IBRD: US 15.98% · Japan 6.88% · China 5.75%. MIGA: US 14.81%.
*The insurer that protects you against a state is governed by states.*

# Does influence have a price? {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## The Security Council in five facts

1. **Five permanent** — China, France, Russia, UK, US — and **ten elected** (six before 1966)
2. Elected for **two years**, five each year, by regional group, two-thirds of the General Assembly; no immediate re-election
3. Substantive decisions: **nine votes, no veto**
4. **Chapter VII** measures bind **every UN member state** — and every firm in them
5. The P5 need nine votes → an elected member's vote **can be pivotal**

## The question

> **Do powerful states pay for the votes of elected Security Council members?**

::: {.muted}
Kuziemko, I., & Werker, E. (2006). *Journal of Political Economy*, 114(5), 905–930. [doi:10.1086/507155](https://doi.org/10.1086/507155)
:::

## The identification idea

::: {.step}
Rotation follows **regional queues and norms**, not a country's need for aid.
:::

So compare a country **with itself**:

| Event time | −3 | −2 | −1 | **0** | **+1** | +2 | +3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | before | before | election year | **term** | **term** | after | after |

::: {.get}
If aid rises in years 0 and +1 and falls back afterwards, the **seat** is the likeliest explanation — not poverty, alliances or politics, which do not rotate.
:::

## What they find

- **US aid rises substantially** during the term — about **59%** in the abstract's headline estimate; UN aid rises more modestly
- The increase is **concentrated in the term** and **disappears afterwards**
- It is **larger when the Council matters more** — measured by press coverage of the Council

::: {.warn}
The salience result turns a correlation into a mechanism. Why?
:::

## From the Council to the banks

::::: columns

:::: {.column width="50%"}

### The finding

Aid moves with membership — and with the salience of Council business. *Vote buying* is the most plausible reading, not a proof of bribery.

::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}

### The bridge

Council members also get more **World Bank** projects and softer **IMF** conditions (Dreher, Sturm & Vreeland 2009a, 2009b); World Bank disbursements track alignment with the US (Kilby 2009).

::::

:::::

::: {.get}
**Who holds the votes shapes who gets the money — and so where the contracts are.**
:::

# The regional development banks {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Same model, different shareholders {.scrollable}

| Bank | Founded · members | Largest shareholders | Firm's window | Who may bid |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **ADB** | 1966 · 69 | Japan 15.6%, US 15.6% | Non-sovereign; Trade & Supply Chain Finance | members |
| **AfDB** | 1964 · 81 | Nigeria 8.8%, US 6.6% (votes) | Private sector; Trade Finance Program | members (ADF: all) |
| **IDB / IDB Invest** | 1959 · 48 | US ≈30% (votes) | IDB Invest; "originate-to-share" | members |
| **EBRD** | 1991 · 77 + EU + EIB | US 10.1% | 75% private sector; Trade Facilitation | **all** |
| **EIB** | 1958 · EU-27 | DE, FR, IT 18.8% each | Loans, equity, guarantees | all |
| **IsDB** | 1975 · 57 | Saudi Arabia 22.5% | ICD, ITFC, ICIEC insurance | mainly members |

::: {.muted}
Plus **CAF** (1968, Latin America) and the **Eurasian Development Bank** (2006, Russia + Kazakhstan + five). Banks' own reports, accessed 16 Oct 2026.
:::

## Three signals in the table

1. **Procurement eligibility is foreign policy** — your home state's shareholding decides whether you may bid
2. **The EBRD suspended Russia and Belarus** on 4 April 2022 — still shareholders, no access
3. **Shareholding moves** — the EBRD into sub-Saharan Africa (2025); the ADB's first Charter amendment (2026)

# The new institutions {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## The AIIB and the NDB {.scrollable}

| | **AIIB** | **NDB** |
|---|---|---|
| **Founded** | Articles 29 June 2015; opened 16 Jan 2016 · Beijing | Fortaleza, 15 July 2014; in force July 2015 · Shanghai |
| **Members** | 111 approved (106 full) — **no US, no Japan** | 5 founders + Bangladesh, UAE, Egypt, Algeria, Uzbekistan |
| **Capital** | US$100 bn authorised | US$100 bn authorised; US$50 bn subscribed **equally** |
| **Votes** | **China 26.37%** vs ¾ supermajority → **veto**; India 7.53%, Russia 5.92% | Equal among founders; founders ≥ 55% |
| **For firms** | Non-sovereign loans, local currencies; co-financing with WB and ADB | Target 30% local-currency financing |

::: {.muted}
AIIB members table; NDB Agreement and members page. Accessed 16 Oct 2026.
:::

## Reserve pools and policy banks {.scrollable}

| | |
|---|---|
| **BRICS CRA** (2014) | US$100 bn: China 41, Brazil/India/Russia 18 each, South Africa 5 · **30%** usable without the IMF |
| **CMIM** (2010) + **AMRO** | ASEAN+3 · US$240 bn of swaps · **40%** IMF-delinked since 2021 |
| **China Development Bank, China Exim** (1994) | Bilateral, state-owned; the core of Belt and Road lending |
| **Silk Road Fund** (Dec 2014) | US$40 bn + RMB 100 bn (2017) |
| **Belt and Road** (2013) | Cooperation documents with 150+ countries · AidData: **US$1.34 trn**, 2000–2021, 165 countries |

# Complement or counter-hegemony? {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Four tests

| | Complement | Counter-hegemony |
|---|---|---|
| **Votes** | Voice the IMF did not give | China's AIIB veto mirrors the US IMF veto |
| **Standards** | AIIB co-financing with WB and ADB from 2016 | Bilateral lending outside OECD rules and cross-debarment |
| **Currency** | Local-currency loans cut mismatch | Settlement outside the dollar |
| **Sanctions** | **2022: AIIB and NDB froze Russia** | CRA, CMIM: crisis money outside the IMF |

::: {.get}
Both. The new banks are an **outside option** — and the more forums there are, the more a host state can shop among them.
:::

# What it means for the firm {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Four channels {.scrollable}

| Channel | Old | New | The firm |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Procurement** | WB, ADB, AfDB, IDB, EBRD, EIB | AIIB, NDB; Chinese-financed projects | track notices; check eligibility |
| **Finance** | IFC, IDB Invest, EBRD, MCPP | AIIB, NDB non-sovereign, local currency | a bank in the capital structure |
| **Insurance** | MIGA, Guarantee Platform, ICIEC | Chinese export-credit insurance | transfer, expropriation, war, contract |
| **Disputes** | ICSID, BITs | none comparable | a treaty-protected structure |

## Five risks — and the lesson

1. **Conditionality** — programmes change the host's policy mix; lending follows politics
2. **Sanctions exposure** — suspension (EBRD), freezes (AIIB, NDB), cross-debarment
3. **Alignment** — BRICS, AIIB, Belt and Road as signals (Session 04)
4. **Competing standards** — bankable for one lender, not for another
5. **Exit** — ICSID denunciations; suspended members

::: {.get}
An institution is a risk **mitigator** when its coalition is stable, and a risk **source** when it is not. **Track the coalition, not just the rule.**
:::

> **Put it to the room:** AIIB co-finances, MIGA insures; the host is sanctioned next year. Who keeps its commitments?

# The Tableau skill of the day {background-color="#E3120B" style="color:#F7F4ED"}

## Years relative to a term

**Join** the **term table** (one row per term) to the **aid table** (country × year) on `Iso3` — a join, not a relationship: row-level calculations cannot mix related tables.

```text
[Event time] = [Year] - [Term start]
```

::: {.warn}
A country with two terms close together appears twice in some years. Overlapping windows: log it.
:::

## A baseline that ignores the view — `FIXED`

```text
[Baseline aid] = { FIXED [Iso3], [Term start] :
                   AVG( IF [Event time] >= -3 AND [Event time] <= -1
                        THEN [Aid] END ) }

[Aid relative to baseline] = [Aid] / [Baseline aid]      // row level: one value per country-year-term
```

::: {.step}
`FIXED` computes at country × term, whatever is on Rows and Columns — so one chart can average across terms a ratio computed **within** each term.
:::
